name: Fougere fragrance family

card.summary: A classic lavender, oakmoss and coumarin scent family whose clean, barbershop character is used to add a polished, groomed impression.
card.note: Oakmoss and some fragrance ingredients can trigger contact allergy in sensitive skin.

quick.overview:
Fougère (French for "fern") is one of the main perfume families. Its recognisable accord pairs bright lavender with mossy oakmoss and hay-like coumarin, giving the fresh, clean, slightly herbal smell associated with barbershops and traditional men's grooming products.[1]

For appearance, scent works as part of the overall impression of being well groomed. People who wear fougères use them as a finishing step alongside a haircut, shave and clothing, and the family's familiar, clean character is part of why it became a standard choice for men's fragrance.[1]
quick.how: Fougère-style scents come as eau de toilette, cologne, aftershave and balms. Many men's classics, such as Brut, Drakkar Noir and Kouros, sit in the family, and modern versions add vetiver, geranium, bergamot, herbs, spice or wood.[1] Wearers typically apply fragrance to skin after showering or shaving.
quick.risks: Fragrance ingredients, including oakmoss, are a known source of contact skin reactions in some people, and alcohol-based products can sting freshly shaved skin. Fragrance preference is personal and varies by setting and culture.

lead: The fougère family is one of the major categories of perfume. Its name is French for "fern", although the accord does not smell of ferns; it is built on lavender in the top, with oakmoss and coumarin (a hay-like note) underneath, often joined by vetiver, geranium or bergamot.[1]

People interested in grooming use fougère scents as part of a clean, polished presentation. The lavender-and-wood profile recalls traditional barbershop products, which is why the family is closely tied to men's aftershaves and colognes.[1]

The family takes its name from Fougère Royale, created in 1882 by Houbigant with perfumer Paul Parquet. It is considered one of the first modern perfumes because it used synthetic aroma chemicals, notably coumarin, which had been synthesised in 1868.[1]

chain: Reads as well groomed alongside hair, skin and clothing
angle.text: Fougères are worn as a finishing touch to grooming. Their clean, familiar barbershop character is used to complement a fresh haircut and shave rather than to change anyone's physical features.

paras: A classic fougère opens with sweet, floral lavender, then moves to a woody, slightly sharp oakmoss note and coumarin, which smells like cut hay. Bergamot can add sharpness, and vetiver or geranium are common additions. Aromatic fougères add herbs, spice or wood.[1]

Houbigant's Fougère Royale (1882), made with Paul Parquet, gave the family its name. It was first aimed at women but became popular with refined urban men, including the writer Guy de Maupassant, who praised it.[1] It was discontinued in the 1950s, its accord was widely reused, and Houbigant reintroduced it in 2010; a copy is held at the Osmothèque in Versailles.[1]

Guerlain's Jicky (1889), often described as the oldest perfume still in continuous production, added synthetic vanillin and coumarin to the fougère accord.[1] Later men's classics in the family include Brut, Drakkar Noir, Kouros, Azzaro Pour Homme and Eternity for Men, while modern entries such as Libre by Yves Saint Laurent have brought the style to women's and unisex perfumery.[1]
Because lavender, wood and herbal notes recall barbershop products, fougères became especially popular as men's fragrances and are strongly linked with men's grooming lines.[1]

timeline.event: Coumarin is first synthesised, later central to the fougère accord.[1]
Houbigant releases Fougère Royale, naming the family.[1]
